# VOLUME 04 — BATCH 0001, CHAPTERS 148–157, MOVEMENT 1: NINE DAYS OF WATER

**Ten chapters, days 251–268, the eleventh to the twenty-eighth of the ninth month. This is the first prose in Volume 04 and it is the whole of Movement 1. The volume's outline is `outline/volume-04.md` and the governing prompt for the next batch is `workspace/volume-04/batch-0002/PROMPT.md`.**

- **148 — *The Eleventh*** — days 251–252, the eleventh and the twelfth, a Friday and a Saturday. **A month opens and the ninth month's compost line is not entered and the reason is entered, and the boards are at one hundred and eighty-five and the tin at two hundred and thirty-two, both cut out loud after the reader of this body makes the clerk read the rule first, which is now the third reading day he has done that on and nobody asked for it.** Then the batch's first act of arithmetic that is about a road and not about money: **the waggon that left on the seventh at about the sixth hour in the afternoon is at the top of the plateau road tonight on four days up and can be in this yard on the fifteenth on four days down, and the entry is that this holding can compute a date and cannot compute a cargo and the two are about the same vehicle and one of them is worth nothing.** Then **a bill**, brought up the fen road on foot by a woman of a household in the low quarter, written on the back of a miller's tally, in four lines, and she says four words before anybody reads it and the four words are *this is a bill*: four wells off since the twenty-first of a month, forty-one houses, **a man hauls at a shilling the pail and has hauled ninety-five a day since the first of this month and not one day less, counted at a gate by four households in turns and the count is theirs and not his**, **eleven days at ninety-five is one thousand and forty-five pails and one thousand and forty-five shillings is fifty-two pounds and five shillings, and the same quarter had nine hundred and ten pails in the whole of last month at the same shilling, which is forty-five pounds and ten shillings**, and the fourth line, **we are not asking this body for anything.** Anneke Roos does the sum three times in the open and then does the other half, **which is that a tin at four pounds and fivepence, a compost line at ninety-five pounds a month and a water bill for a quarter nine miles off are three kinds of number and are not added to each other**, and she projects the bill to the thirtieth at two thousand eight hundred and fifty pails and one hundred and forty-two pounds ten. And then the batch's argument: **a name is a thing other people can spend, and a body which is a name has stopped being able to say no, because a thing that has a name has somebody to blame and a thing that has not got a name has to go and do the work — and this holding has been a name for about nine days and nobody in the yard saw it arrive.** Nobody said the second thing right either. The woman from the low quarter was in that yard for two hours and nobody asked her anything and she was not thanked and did not ask to be. Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **149 — *A Party And Not A Holder*** — days 253–254, the thirteenth and the fourteenth, a Sunday and a Monday. **The trust's guarantee arrives on the ordinary post with the bill and is read in a room on the Sunday, because a definition is read in a room and this is a guarantee and a guarantee is a thing people sign.** Four clauses and a schedule of eleven numbers, written on the second and nine days back on the March road: the trust stands behind the seed and its cost **for planting in ground with a named return**; **the guarantee is given to the holder of the well named at the foot and to no other person and no other body**; **where there is no holder the trust's duty is to the seed and not to the water**; **and the receipt is to be given by the person who plants and not by the holder of the well.** At the foot: **the Pans well, on the dry road, eleven miles. The holder of record, Garrow Nye, of no address this office holds.** The second clause is read out three times in a room of nine and the count is entered. The reader of this body then says the thing the volume is about and says that the sheet is the most ordinary paper that has come into this building in a year, **and that the correct reading of it is that a body of sixteen households on one head is not a party to it, and the reason is on the face of the sheet, in the second clause, in the ordinary way, and nobody in that room has to be told anything by anybody** — and that the one sentence he could not find for three readings is **the trust's duty is to the seed and not to the water**, and he would like somebody in four years to tell him whether that was arrogance or the only way it can be written. Tova Reed refuses the conversion in the form she refuses in, **a thing that one person can do is not a thing a body can be asked to do**, fifth time, and gives the reason in the form of a form: **a guarantee of seed given to a body that cannot hold water is a promise about somebody else's water, made by people who cannot be there when it is not there, and if that promise fails the trust will hear about it nine days later on a road and the households will have heard about it in a yard the same afternoon.** And she gives the two prices: **thirty-one shillings and fourpence a hundredweight at Cray on the second, eleven shillings in a yard at Fennmere on the ninth, a difference of twenty shillings and fourpence, which is the price of a road and not the price of hunger, and a road price can be refused by a person who has seed in her own ground and a hunger price cannot — and nine thousand people in the March are going to walk, and the only thing anybody has told her that any of them is walking toward is a road with a well at the bottom of it that is somebody's.** Lissa Vale, unforgiven and unthanked, asks the only question in the room that is hers: **clause four gives a receipt to the person who plants and not to the holder, and that is the first instrument in eleven years in which a grower is a party without holding a well, and it arrived here by accident, on a Sunday, in the rain — and this holding will not put the trust's seed into one head with a leak and a beat and a draw it is still paying for.** Then, on the Monday, at the gate, in the ordinary business of a figure and not on anything else: **give me the number on the sixteenth — you will have it on the twenty-first — enter it as the twenty-first**, and the clerk enters that a date is not a figure and that **the count of figures this holding has been given a date for and not received is one, and that the count is entered before the figure rather than after it.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **150 — *Four Days Down*** — day 255, the fifteenth, a Tuesday. **The waggon is in the yard at about the seventh hour, four days down, and the reader of this body says the fifteenth out loud again before anybody has got out of the cart and then says, in the same breath, that being right about a road does not make a man right, and asks the clerk to enter the whole sentence.** There are **nine people and a seed chest of twenty-six trays, lashed with a rope tied and untied and tied again, and a tenth person who is not one of the nine.** **Soren Rill, a guide, of an assembly of people who live in the old wood up the coast road, not here as a representative of anybody, with no paper that says so, and who asks that the words *said a thing* be in the writing and not the word *sent*.** And then, before the cloth comes off the chest, **in his first hour, unasked: there is a living root in the low ground at the bottom of this road and I will not have a crew across it, and I would rather say that in the first hour than on the fourth day, and this is not an accusation against anybody in this yard and I have not made one.** The reader asks the only question nobody else in that yard could ask — **say what a living root is and say how a man would know** — and is answered: **he will not give a definition, because a definition would be a thing you could check, and what he has is not that; a shape of ground; a held ground and a dead ground do not look the same to a man who has looked at a lot of it and look the same to everybody else, and that is worth nothing in a hearing. And then the part that can be checked: the ground has been in that shape longer than the charter on the well at the bottom of the other road, and he will not put a year on his reading of it, and he has read four pieces of ground in nine years and three of them were crews with a licence and a schedule, and in none of the three did the schedule say that what was being held was being held because somebody was doing work on it every day. And the fourth had nobody in it, is down the coast road, he has not been back, and he will not say what he found there.** The count of noes goes to **five**, and the entry says the fifth is not a body and has no ledger and cannot be written to, and the count is entered anyway. Then the woman with the chest says where they came from and where they are going in nine sentences: **thirty-one of them at Tolbury, twenty-six trays, not one left there, four days of water carried six days, and the coast road because the coast road has a bridge at the third crossing and the fen road has one at the first and the fen road is eleven miles longer and there is no second bridge between here and the water** — and she says four times on the road that they are not asking for anything and a fifth time in this yard. The reader then says the true thing out loud, to them and not to us: **nothing. There is nothing in this body for you, and if any man in this yard offers you a bed tonight he is speaking for himself and not for this holding.** **Nobody offered them a bed.** The nine went down the road in the rain and were offered nothing and did not ask, and about twenty-five people from this head were in that yard and the count of households on this road that have not moved is still two hundred and eighty. Then the two figures of the engineer of record: **he went down four hundred yards below the gate with a rule for fifty minutes, wrote nine feet two inches in his own book, read it out when he was asked, and when he was asked whether that was the figure he answered that it was a figure — both answers entered in the order given, and the reader did not ask which of the two he would have got if he had asked the second question first, and entered that he did not ask and did not say why.** And the tenth person is still in the yard at the eleventh hour, having said he was not going to the fen, and the reader enters that he is not going to ask him the next question in the rain and that he had not decided whether he was allowed to. Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **151 — *The Sixteenth*** — day 256, the sixteenth, a Wednesday. **The volume's first clock, and the whole chapter is narrated from outside, four hundred miles off, at the fourth hour, in a yard of four households, by the occupier, with her own nail and her own string.** **The reading is five feet and one inch.** She says the whole of it in about a minute and a half: the reading, and the second half, which is what it is a reading of, and the wall — **and the wall is copied out entire on the page, eight lines in her hand, and under the last one, in the same chalk, the only sentence on that wall that is not a figure: *I do not write what it is made of. A. Ollvar.*** The series: nine feet on the sixteenth of a month four months back, five feet and a half on the fourteenth, five feet five inches on the sixteenth, five feet four inches on the twentieth, five feet two inches on the thirtieth, five feet three inches on the sixteenth of a month two months back, five feet two inches on the sixteenth of last month, five feet and one inch on the sixteenth. **And nine feet less five feet and one inch is three feet and eleven inches, and that is what a person writes on a wall and nothing else, and she has not written what the three feet and eleven inches is made of because she does not know and because the last woman who told her she knew was telling her a thing she had heard** — and the reason is on the page and is not modesty: **a wall is for ever and a woman in a yard is not, and if I put a reason on that wall then in four years there will be a reason on that wall and a nail and a string, and a person will come along and read the reason and skip the nail.** And: **there is no entry on that wall for this well coming back and there is not going to be one from me, and I have been asked three times in a season by men off the low road and I have said no three times and I am going to say it a fourth time for the wall — a well is a nail and a string, and if you have needed me to tell you what a well is for then you have come to the wrong yard.** Then the ordinary day: the grass cut every ten days, a stone put back into the west wall on the fourteenth, **and a place in the stack against the north wall where a thing stood for thirty-one years and does not stand now, and the four of them have not agreed on a name for the place and none of the four will say what the thing was.** **And in the first row the cuttings the man with the spade left on the ground are still lying on the ground, with two stakes at the two faces that were not read, and in the older row, the row nobody has read with a rule and a lens, there is green coming up out of the collars.** The occupier's whole answer, four sentences, to a man who wants a reason for the wall: **a thing comes up where nobody is doing anything to it. That is not a finding. That is the difference between a thing and a finding and I have watched two men in my life not know it.** Three of the four looked; the fourth has not and said once that he is not going to. **Nobody dug, nobody weighed it, nothing came off that shelf in a vessel, nobody has said what it is, and nobody has said that the telling is still going on and nobody has said that it has stopped.** And the **day letter was off its stone from the morning of the eighth to the evening of the seventeenth, eight days of nothing in it, found by the man with the spade on a shelf above the fire**, with four reasons given and the four are not the same reason and the fourth is **I took it**, and he would say nothing else and one of the four did not ask him twice, and **the eight days were not entered on it and this fen was not told for four days and has not written and asked.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **152 — *Ninety-Four*** — days 257–258, the seventeenth and the eighteenth. **Three places, one pail, and the entry goes in before the figures: a pail is not a measure, a count of strokes is a count of strokes, and these three figures are three counts and not a rate and not a head and not a yield.** The examiner keeps the time and does not round and says so in the low quarter in front of nine people who were not told she was coming. **Ninety-four at this holding's own head, a hundred and fifty-one at a well in the low quarter nine miles off, two hundred and nine at the Pans well eleven miles off on the eighteenth.** And then the batch's best scene of work: **in that yard four men said the same sentence in the same words — *Is the road taking it off us?* — and not one of the other forty-odd people said anything, and the engineer of record answered the same question four times in the same words, and gave the reason for answering it the same way each time: *I have got a pail and a watch and I have not got an answer, and I am not going to give you one today, and I would rather say that than give you a figure that belongs to me.*** And to the second question, *then who is taking it off us*: **I do not know, and I have not got a charter and I have got no standing on that road, and if I told you a name I would be telling you a name I got from a sheet with no address on it, and that would be worse than nothing, because you would use it and I would have given it to you for free.** The count of men who have said that sentence is **four** and the count of people in the quarter is **four hundred and forty-one** and the fen is not going to divide one into the other. Then the differences, named before the result: **fifty-seven, a hundred and fifteen, fifty-eight**, and **two hundred and nine against ninety-four is two and a bit times and not two and a quarter times, because two and a quarter times ninety-four is two hundred and eleven and a half and this body does not have that number.** Jonas Byre says the sentence he has been chewing on since the sixth hour, about his own cough and not about anybody else, and it is not made a finding: **the well in that quarter is slower than this holding's own head, and this holding's own head has been on a leak of five-eighths since before the flood and has a beat in it and had a draw out of it on the twelfth of last month, and the two numbers do not fit any story I have been told in eleven years, and the one they do fit is that the water under that quarter was never as good as anybody in it believed and somebody has been selling them the difference for a season.** The reader enters that it is a sentence made and not a finding, **and gives the reason, which is that a man who has timed a pail twice has established a count and has not established where the water came from, and the difference between those two is the whole of the last two volumes of this book and this body has been on the wrong side of it more than once.** And then the frame of the whole volume, said in a yard of about nine: **a man is not stealing from a quarter, he is emptying a well, and taking a thing that belongs to somebody is theft and everybody in this yard knows what to do about it, and drawing a thing out of a place until the place stops, and charging by the pail, and being a man with a cart and not a man with a licence, is a supply, and a supply is a thing the law has an opinion about and the law is nine miles away in a building and does not live in a yard. And if we say he is a thief then the next thing anybody in that quarter will say is that the well was always ours, and the well was not always ours, and there is a charter on it and the charter is somebody's.** The count of questions asked in a yard and not got an answer is **two**. The **forty-third** note goes in on the eighteenth, dated, read back before it was initialled. Panel: none. Notes: the **forty-third**, dated **the eighteenth**, **carrying the standing sentence.**
- **153 — *A Return In The Ordinary Course*** — days 259–260, the nineteenth and the twentieth, a Saturday and a Sunday. **The batch's third document: four lines from the sub-office at Fennmere, on the ordinary post, on the eighteenth, signed at the foot by the desk and not by a person, and it is correct.** **A licensed holder of a well may supply water to a quarter in which wells are off, and a supply so made is a licensed use and is entered as one. The rate is one shilling and fourpence the hundredweight, of which seven pence is the tariff and nine pence is the holder's. The parties to a supply are to be identified and returned on the form provided. And this return is made in the ordinary course and no part of it is a finding against any person, and nothing in this line states that any water has been taken by anybody who was not entitled to take it.** Read in a room, and the fourth line read twice, and the arithmetic done **before** the fourth line and said so. **A pail is not a hundredweight and the two have been carried as one for a month, and that carrying is entered as a practice and not as a fact, and this body can check neither.** The margin, derived twice and said so, with the first derivation wrong and admitted: **one thousand and forty-five hundredweight at sixteen pence is sixteen thousand seven hundred and twenty pence, which is sixty-nine pounds and thirteen shillings and fourpence, against fifty-two pounds and five shillings paid, so the difference is seventeen pounds, eight shillings and fourpence — and fourpence a hundredweight on one thousand and forty-five hundredweight is four thousand one hundred and eighty pence, which is three hundred and forty-eight shillings and fourpence — and that is a road and is in nobody's pocket and is the price of eleven miles.** Then what the sheet does, said standing, with the reason first: **nobody in that room has been accused of anything, and in about four days there is going to be a person on this fen road who says this holding took water that was not its own, and he will be quoting this sheet, and he will be quoting it correctly.** And: **it makes the water in that quarter a licensed thing and the people in it the households served by a licensed well, and it asks for the parties to be identified — and this body is a party. Not a holder. A party. And that is the standing this holding has been proud of on the first of a month, and it is the standing that makes this form ours, and there is no version of the eleventh of this month in which the bill that came up that gate was anybody else's.** The count of noes goes to **six** with the reason entered: **we cannot name a single party to a licensed supply in the low quarter and we will not try, and the reason is that there are four hundred and forty-one people in that quarter and we do not know which of them bought a pail and which of them was given one, and a form that asks us to say would make us the people who know** — and **the difference between not knowing and refusing has been the whole argument of this book for a year and is not going to be collapsed in a month because a piece of paper came in the post.** Who loses, answered by the man of the north row with the cough and not by the steward: **one, the low quarter. Two, the hundred and forty-five households on this road that have not moved, who are about to be asked to fill in a form about somebody else's water. And three, and I am the man who has to say it: the man with the cart, who is losing nothing and is the only one of the three who is winning, and who does not know that he is in a book.** And the man of thirty-five was at the wall side of that yard for two hours and said nothing and was not asked. Then Sunday: **the sheet from the fourth house, written on the sixteenth at the fourth house, down the four-day road, in the occupier's hand, at that household's cost, which is the first time in a season that this body has been beaten home by a household's own expense and the fourth time and the count is entered.** Four lines: the reading and *I have not written what the difference is made of and I am not going to*; the day letter and *we have not written the eight days and I am telling you that we have not and I am not going to tell you why not*; the green and *we have not dug at it and we have not weighed it and nothing has come off this shelf in a vessel, and nobody here has said what it is*; **and the fourth: the man with the spade has not spoken to the other three since the seventeenth, we have not asked him, and we are telling you because you are the only party we have that writes things down.** And the answer, which is the chapter's last line of business: **we cannot write to them, not because of the money; there is no form on which this body can put a line about a man who has not spoken to three people four hundred miles off, and no address on the sheet, and I have looked and there is not one and I am not going to invent a way of writing in order to have the feeling of having written. So the fourth line is on the page and it is a fact about a yard, and the word nothing is entered four times.** And the third figure from the engineer of record, given on the twentieth to a fourth person, **and this body has not got it and is not going to ask for it until somebody asks him in a yard where the clerk is standing.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **154 — *A Place Can Be Dry*** — day 261, the twenty-first, a Monday. **The batch's one Fieldbook panel, spent at the fourth hour, at a contact on a boarded floor over a shaft in this holding's own low ground that came off on the twenty-first of a month two months back.** The use log's **fourteenth line** written first and read back twice, the contact tested with a plain wire gauge and the reading of the test written down before the instrument was laid on the boards, and **the fieldbook is not in the case and is four hundred miles off in a room with a lock, and the instrument is not the book and the two have been confused in a room in this book before.** The panel, four lines and not three, because the instrument reads a node and has never read a page: *This is not the same as the mouth. / A place can be dry and not be empty. / What is under a floor is not under your hand. / Ground that is held is ground somebody is working.* And the cost: **the mark hot for the rest of the day, the hand from the wrist down no use for about a day, the case carried up the slope by the man from the north row because he asked and nobody else offered in time, and the rootmark is four inches and branching twice and is not longer this morning than it was on the eleventh.** What he can defend and what he cannot, in that order, and the thing he is not going to say: **I am not going to say anybody is working down there. A thing being held is a fact about the thing and not about a person.** Then, at the sixth hour, the man with the cart: **the Pans well stopped at the fourth hour yesterday morning and there was nothing in the bucket that was not in the bottom of the bucket, and the holder's man came out at the seventh hour and has not said anything that could be repeated and was not asked, and I am telling you and not the district and I did not come nine miles for a form.** The reader asks him to say what he is so that the clerk can enter it as a function: **I haul, and I have never been anything but a man with a cart, and I am not going to be asked to be anything else, because the last time somebody asked me to be something else I said yes and then I could not stop saying it.** And then the volume's three facts in a yard, and the reader saying the ordinary thing **before** anybody else: **a body that has been a name for nine days has three facts in front of it today and all three are about water, and the ordinary thing a named body does with three facts about water is to go and get some, and I would like the clerk to enter that I said that before anybody else in this yard did.** And then the door, read whole at the tenth hour in a full yard of about twenty-five, **the seventh column at thirty-one**, and the figures: no compost line, **the leak at three-quarters of an inch read twice with two rules and no cause and no due date, and the reading of the thirteenth of a month two months back is five-eighths, and this body will not say whether the difference between those two figures is a movement or a season**, the beat not logged since with the column open, **and the new entry that the rule's third line does not say in a yard and this body read it as though it did for two years and the rule has no clause for that and there is no fifth line and there never has been one**, the boards at one hundred and ninety-five, the tin at two hundred and forty-two. And the standing rule read out again in full, four lines, and the last thing in that yard, said with his hand flat on the bench: **the first line says the draw is not begun on ground whose return is not carrying, and nobody in this yard can say whether the return under that floor is carrying, because the instrument said the ground is held and the man of about thirty-five says a held ground is ground somebody is working, and he is not in this yard, is not a licensed man, has no book, and is not a party to this body and cannot be asked in a room and be made to give an answer that goes in a book. So the rule cannot be satisfied tomorrow morning and the rule has got no clause for a rule that cannot be satisfied — and here is the reason I read the rule out again today and it is not a good reason: a rule that stops a man by asking a question only one stranger can answer is a rule that has handed him the whole of it, and I am the man who wrote it.** Panel: the one available, spent here. Notes: none.
- **155 — *Four Feet*** — days 262–263, the twenty-second and the twenty-third. **The draw is begun at the fourth hour and twenty minutes of the twenty-second on the boarded floor, with about four people on the boards and no yard called, and the rule does not say a yard has to be called.** The night before, in a room with four people in it, the reader of this body enters the fault that is the chapter's whole engine: **the third line does not say in a yard; for two years this yard has read that line as though it said so, including me and including the clerk, and the entry has been made as though it were the line — and so the rule was used outside one of its own four lines because this holding built a custom of calling a yard and put the custom in its own mouth and never in its own book, and the cost of that is four feet out of a floor with four people on it and about nine people asleep a quarter of a mile away, and I have got no figure and am not going to get one.** The stop is called at the fourth hour and forty minutes **at four feet, by a licensed man, in a low ground with about four people in it, entered by the licensed man in his own hand with the hour on it**, and the fourth line kept: **the person who called the stop is not the person who did the work**, and a rule read after the thing it governs is a report and a rule read before is a rule. Then the cost, in the plainest words the yard could manage: **darkened veins past the mark into the elbow from about the fifth hour of the twenty-second until about the third hour of the twenty-fourth; fever twice in the night; numbness in three fingers, the two middle ones and the ring one, and the third finger is the one he rules with; loss of taste from the eleventh hour of the twenty-second until the ninth hour of the twenty-third; the hand no use from the wrist down for two days, and the man from the north row carried the rule and the case and the examiner carried the pail, and he was told once that the boards were wet and not twice, and the count of times he needed to be told is not entered and cannot be entered by anybody but him.** **The two accounts of the arm do not agree and were not reconciled: a day and a half, or two, and an hour at about the fourth that is in neither.** And the miller's board, four lines, with **a fourth line carrying no figure at all, the first such line in nineteen years of that board**: two hundred and forty-four on the sixteenth, two hundred and forty-four on the morning of the twenty-second, two hundred and thirty-three on the morning of the twenty-third, **and the wheel was not turned by the water on the morning of the twenty-second and I turned it by my own arm for a count of ninety**. Eleven, entered as a difference and not a cause. Then the thing with people attached to it: **a woman of a household in the low quarter came up on foot on the twenty-third and did not stop at the gate and came the last four hundred yards down into the low ground, and said four things and the fourth was not about herself — the well they were drawing off went off at about the second hour; we do not know that it is you and I want that said first, because I have had four men say the other thing at me in four days and I am not going to be the fifth; but I timed it, one hundred and fifty-one every day since the seventeenth, and this morning I could not get a pail of it and I stood in that yard for about an hour and a half and timed it four times and there was nothing to time; and there were five houses on our row that had water on the fourteenth and there are four, and the one that went is not ours, and the man with the cart has been in that yard since the fifth hour and has not said where the water comes from and I did not ask him, because he is a man with a cart and I am a woman with a pail, and that is how it is done down there and it is not going to be me who changes it this week.** And the engineer of record, asked who loses, answering for the first time in ten chapters and refusing the sum: **I did it. I began it at twenty past four in the morning on a floor over a shaft with four people on the boards and no yard called, and I did not tell anybody in this holding that I was going to do it — and the reason is that I did not want a yard, and it took me a day and a half to get to the words, because I knew what the rule's first line said and I knew I could not satisfy it, and the only way I could get past that without breaking the rule in front of anybody was to do it when there was nobody there to break it in front of, and that is a thing you do when you have decided you are going to do a thing and not a thing you do when you have decided the right thing.** Nobody answered him and nobody was asked, **and the fen entered that this is NOT one of the six noes, in a separate line on purpose, because a thing a man does to himself is not a refusal and must not be counted as one.** And the man of about thirty-five, who had said nothing for a day and a half, said one sentence and went up the slope: **a held ground and a dry ground are not the same, and I told you that on the fifteenth and you have been down there twice since and asked a piece of metal instead of asking me — but a held ground does not empty in a morning and does not come back in an afternoon, and if a well nine miles off went off the same day you took four feet, then that well was not on the same ground, and you have got a floor under a shaft and a well nine miles off and a road eleven miles off and you have put them in one book and one of them is not yours.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **156 — *The Word He Would Not Let Them Have*** — days 264–265, the twenty-fourth and the twenty-fifth. **At the fourth hour of the twenty-fourth the man of about thirty-five comes down into the low ground on foot and gives the reason he came at that hour before he gives anything else: he did not come on the twenty-second because the engineer of record was on it and he does not come into a thing while a man is in it, and he would rather say it to a man on a floor than to a yard, because a yard will write it down and a floor will not.** Then the refusal, with the source named and the speaker named: **on the twenty-third, at the wall side of this ground, the man from the north row with the cough said the word nest, once, not to anybody, and I was four feet away and I heard it.** And the reason, and it is the best piece of reasoning in the batch: **I am not going to pretend to you that I do not know what he meant, because I do know and because you would not believe a man who did not know. A nest is a thing a thing makes when it is stopping. That is what a nest is. It is a place a thing builds and then stays in, and it is not a road and it is not a queue and it is not a thing that is on its way anywhere. A nest has one thing in it and one thing in it has a number. What is under that ground is not that. I have read that ground four times and it is not one thing, and the reason I know it is not one thing is that I have watched it refuse — in a year I am not going to name, a crew with a licence and a schedule put a probe into it, and the ground closed over the probe and took the schedule with it and the schedule came up in a different place eleven feet on, and I have never in my life seen a thing do that twice, and I have been waiting two years to see it do it twice and it did not. So there is no number under that ground. And a thing with no number under it and a road on it is not a nest, and the word you want is the word for a thing that has to be answered to, and you will not use it because using it means somebody is going to have to answer, and nobody in this district has ever had to answer a thing about a floor.** Somebody asks him what the word is and he says no in one word, and then he gives **the half that is checkable**: **a thing under that ground does not go where the ground goes, and it is doing work, and the work is not water and is not seeds and is not anything anybody in this yard can name, and it is the sort of work that stops if nobody does it.** And he will not say what it is, and he has said no in one word to four offices in nineteen years and has never had to say it twice to the same one. **And then the ask, in nine words, with the reason entered as the reason, which is that there is none he is willing to put in a book of a body of sixteen households on one head.** Lissa Vale asks the only question that is hers to ask — **who brings it back** — and he says **not him**, and the clerk is told to enter it in the form he said it and not to let anybody in the book say later that he promised. And then he does the thing nobody expected: **he says the price out loud before anybody asks him to. One pail. And the losing of a man you have had for four days, who has not been paid and is not going to be paid and is not asking, and who has told you two things in a dark yard with a lamp on it that are worth about four years of work to a man who does this. That is the whole of the price and I am telling you in front of four people so that you can decide whether it is one you want to pay, and not one of those four is going to have an opinion and I would like that entered too.** Nobody had an opinion. Then the concealment, at the eleventh hour, in a room with four people of whom one is the clerk: **the engineer of record told the seedwright of the trust that the ground under the low quarter is going to move before the end of next month, and he said the eleventh, and he cannot defend it and has not got a second reading. She said: enter it. He said: I will enter it when I can defend it.** And her sentence, once, and the reader of this body was not in the room and has never read it back: **a thing that is true and in one room is not a secret yet. The day it is in the same room again is the day it is a secret, and I am telling you the day now so that you cannot have it later, and I am not going to be thanked for it and I have said that before I was thanked.** And: **I am not going to write it down, and the reason is that a thing that one person can carry is not a thing a body can be asked to carry, and that is the sixth time in a year I have said a sentence of that shape and the sixth time I have refused to have it written as a refusal.** So there is a date in this book and there is no figure against it. And then the Friday: **a body of sixteen households on one head finds out what it has, which is two pails, counted twice by the examiner on the Friday morning, and one of them belongs to a woman and one of them is carrying three people's work** — and the man of about fifty does the whole of it in about four sentences, the shortest thing he has said in a season: **we have two pails and there is no such pail as this holding's pail, and I am not going to have a yard spend a week on it; we have no pail and never have and I have never once in eleven years counted them and I counted them this morning because a stranger asked for one, and that is the correct order to find things out in and I would like it entered as a fault and not as a lesson; and a pail is not the thing that matters, because he asked for a pail, a measure and an hour, and the pail is the smallest of the three and the hour is the whole of it, and nobody in this yard knows what the hour is for, and I have never once agreed to a thing I could not name.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **157 — *The Hour*** — days 266–268, the twenty-sixth, the twenty-seventh and the twenty-eighth. **The batch's completed beat, and it costs.** On the twenty-sixth at about the third hour of the afternoon, **in a yard with about thirty people in it, which is the largest this holding has had on a working day since the flood, this body gives away a pail, a measure and four hours of a licensed man's time, and enters all three, and the hour is fixed for the fourth hour of the twenty-eighth to the eighth hour of it.** The reader puts them as three things and will not have them put as a gift: **one, this holding has two pails and has had for eleven years and nobody knew until Friday morning when a stranger asked for one, and that is a fault and not a lesson; two, the boards pail, washed, and the wash is entered because the last thing it carried was a man's fever and the man does not want it recorded; three, the pail may not come back, he said so on Thursday in front of four people, the steward asked who would bring it back and he said not him, and nobody in this yard has been given a promise and has been given a time.** Then the steward's second answer this holding has ever given that it could not finish, and it is entered with its reason: **on the seventh of last month I could not tell you what four carts cost anybody, and today I cannot tell you what a held ground costs, what nine people and four days of water cost, what twenty-six trays cost a woman who carried them eleven miles, what seventeen pounds, eight shillings and fourpence of road costs four hundred and forty-one people, or what a man with a cart will do on the twenty-eighth with a pail and an hour. And what has changed is that this holding is now a party to one thing it cannot price, and that is the first time in eleven years I have had to stand in a yard and admit that a thing I have done has a price I have not got.** And a licensed man refuses to go, and the reason is that **a licensed man under a ground is a thing that can be written about afterwards, and I would rather there were four people in this yard who can say afterwards that there was no licensed man under that ground at any hour on the twenty-eighth** — and he will be at both hours and will not write down what happened in between and has not asked. On the twenty-seventh, in a room of nine, **the reader asks the question of the batch: is there anything in this holding's book that you know and that is not in this holding's book — and the engineer of record says yes, and is told not to be asked what it is, and gives the count and the day and not the thing: four answers in a season, and the count of the four that are in this book's book is one, and the fourth one is dated the eleventh of next month.** And the reader says the other half of it first, and it is the volume's fault line: **a man who cannot defend a thing and holds it anyway has not kept a private record, he has started one — and a body that has a name can hold a thing it cannot defend, and that is how a name becomes a party, and I said in a yard on the eleventh of this month that a name is a thing other people can spend, and I did not think about that for nine days and I have thought about it for one, and I would like somebody in four years to find the two pages and read them side by side.** Nobody answered him and nobody was asked. On the twenty-eighth the standing figures are read with nothing softened — **no compost line, the leak at three-quarters with no verdict on the difference, the beat not logged since, the seventh column at thirty-one, the boards at two hundred and two, the tin at two hundred and forty-nine, the rule four lines used once and used outside one of them, the contact and its cost and the rootmark unchanged, the well on the shelf at five feet and one inch and three feet and eleven inches not decomposed, the day letter and the green and the fourth line with nothing entered four times, and a pail, a measure and four hours gone.** **The man of about seventy is fetched for the twelfth time in a season and says three words: write it twice**, and nobody explained it and the fen does not know what it means. And then the volume's third question, in the fen's own words, **and the page is careful that it is not the first two: the first question asks who gave an order, and the third does not ask that, and nobody in this book could answer it, because an order has a person at the end of it and this body has not got one and has looked and not found one.** The count of the times it has been asked is one and the count of the times it has been available to a room and not taken is one, and **the two counts are not to be added to the count of the first question, which stands at two asked and three available and not taken, and the count of a question is the count of a question.** The **forty-fourth** note closes the month and carries the standing sentence. Panel: none. Notes: the **forty-fourth**, dated **the twenty-eighth**, **carrying the standing sentence.**

# VOLUME 04 — BATCH 0002, CHAPTERS 158–167, MOVEMENT 2: WHAT SHE SAID IN A ROOM

**Ten chapters, days 269–285, the twenty-ninth and the thirtieth of the ninth month through the fifteenth of the tenth, and the batch crosses the month turn between Ch 158 and Ch 159 and therefore has TWO naming tables and not one. The volume's outline is `outline/volume-04.md` and the governing prompt for this batch is `workspace/volume-04/batch-0002/PROMPT.md`, which was written by the phase that drafted Batch 0001 and carries the ten cards. - **158 — *The Thirtieth*** — days 269–270, the twenty-ninth and the thirtieth, a Tuesday and a Wednesday. **The batch's first fact is a fact about a floor, told flat and at the front: the hour on the twenty-eighth has run, a licensed man was at the fourth hour and at the eighth and wrote both down, a measure and a plain wire gauge were on the boards at the eighth, the pail was not, and nobody came with either.** Coll Renner gives the hour before the finding and gives the finding before anything else, and puts *nobody came with either* in the same line as the two of them because a person is not what came or did not come. **The reader of this body then splits the sentence in two and has the two halves entered apart: nobody in that yard can say what the hour was for, and that is a fact; the fen has decided this morning not to ask him and not to write to anybody about it, and that is a decision.** The man of about thirty-five has said he will not be asked again by this body and would say no in one word to a person in an office. Then the last reading day of the ninth month: **the door read out whole at the tenth hour in a full yard of about twenty-five, by the steward, with the reader and the clerk, the count of the readings of the seventh column going to thirty-two**, the compost line for the month not entered and the reason entered (**the figure falls on the first of next month, a Thursday, and this holding has said so out loud on the eleventh, the sixteenth, the twenty-first, the twenty-ninth and the thirtieth of the ninth month and the count of the five is entered**), the leak at three-quarters of an inch with no verdict, the beat not logged since with the column open, **the boards at two hundred and four days, day minus sixty-six, and the March's tin at two hundred and fifty-one, day minus nineteen, both cut or read out with the day-minus rule read out loud first, which the reader has now done on four reading days running and which nobody asked for**, and the standing rule read out in full again, four lines, before the door is closed. And then the question the chapter is for, asked standing and not taken: **was the hour.** Nobody answers it, nobody is asked to, and **the count of the questions available to a room in this holding and not taken goes to five**, the first in a month two months back and the fourth in a low ground on the twenty-third, and the reader says he is not going to ask it twice and enters the reason, that he has no standing to ask after it. And the steward's **third answer this holding has ever given that it could not finish**, and the difference between it and the first two is on the page: **the first was what four carts cost, the second was what four hours cost, and this one is what a thing this body cannot ask anybody about cost, and a body that has given away a thing and got half of it back is not in the same position as a body that was refused, and there is no sentence in this book's vocabulary for that and I am not going to invent one in a yard.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **159 — *The First Of The Tenth*** — day 271, the first of the tenth month, a Thursday, which is also the day the ninth month's compost line falls on, and the page says both are on the same day and is not going to make anything of it. The line is entered at about the eleventh hour in a yard of about twenty, by the examiner, in the steward's book, in her own hand, which is not the steward's hand, with the reader appointed being the man of about fifty: **specification four hundred hundredweight; the going, nothing, and the reason entered, that this holding hired nobody in the ninth month and paid off nobody hired in it, and the examiner states she has been in the hiring book twice and did not believe herself the first time; shortfall four hundred hundredweight, eighty pounds, at four shillings the hundredweight, which is the compost valuation and is not anybody's day rate; the run of it is nine months and it has not been discharged in nine.** And the batch's arithmetic beat, said before the figure and without any pleasure in it: **it is emptier, not better — the first month in nine that has not gone up, and it has not gone up because there was nothing in it to charge.** The two sums, not averaged and not in one column: **four hundred at four shillings is one thousand six hundred shillings, eighty pounds; and four hundred at the price at Cray, three shillings and elevenpence, being forty-seven pence, is eighteen thousand eight hundred pence, which is one thousand five hundred and sixty-six shillings and eightpence, seventy-eight pounds six shillings and eightpence; the difference is one pound, thirteen shillings and fourpence, and the whole of that difference is a penny that came down by itself on a sheet with a firm's name at the head of it on the first of last month, and this holding did not cause it and did not write and ask — and a body that puts that penny on the same line as a hundredweight specification is a book that has stopped being a book.** The reader reads the run aloud, ninety pounds eight, eighty pounds eight, ninety-five, eighty, and enters that a fall of fifteen pounds from the month before is not good news and is the same line. Then the batch's whole clock, four sentences at the end: **the reader of this body says the date out loud in a yard of about twenty, in the ordinary voice, and says three days, and the examiner says ten days and not three and says before anything is written down that she keeps time and does not round, and he agrees with her, and both figures are entered and neither is improved on.** He does not say whose date it is and does not say what it is about, and does not ask the engineer of record. **The man of about seventy is at the wall and is not fetched, and is given the two sums, the two figures and the difference, and says nothing, and the fen entered that it did not ask him whether he had anything to say, which is his standing and has never once cost anybody anything.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **160 — *Two And A Bit Times*** — days 272–273, the second and the third, a Friday and a Saturday. **A schedule comes up the fen road on the ordinary post from the holder of record of a well eleven miles off, in a clerk's hand, with the days listed and a figure at the foot, and it is correct, and the holder's man is not on it and the holder is.** Four lines: a supply is made on a day on which the wells of the quarter served are off and is not made on a day on which they are on; **drawn, the first to the eleventh of last month, eleven days, and the nineteen to the twenty-third, five days; sixteen days at ninety-five the hundredweight a day: one thousand five hundred and twenty hundredweight**; and the ordinary-course line with the form outstanding. **The reader finds the seven missing days in the middle and the seven in the tail, and the first line explains them, and then says the thing this holding cannot do about them: it cannot count fourteen days of wells in a quarter of four hundred and forty-one people, and the fourteen days at the top of that sheet are the most checkable-looking part of it and the part this body cannot check at all, and I have read a schedule and I have not read fourteen days of that quarter's ground.** Then the batch's best piece of arithmetic, done twice out loud and both derivations entered: **at one shilling and fourpence, being sixteen pence, one thousand five hundred and twenty hundredweight is twenty-four thousand three hundred and twenty pence, which is two thousand and twenty-six shillings and eightpence, which is one hundred and one pounds, six shillings and eightpence; they paid one thousand five hundred and twenty shillings, which is seventy-six pounds; the difference is twenty-five pounds, six shillings and eightpence. And fourpence a hundredweight on one thousand five hundred and twenty is six thousand and eighty pence, which is five hundred and six shillings and eightpence, which is twenty-five pounds six shillings and eightpence. Same.** And that it is a road, eleven miles, in nobody's pocket, with four hundred and forty-one people at the end of it. And then the half that is the chapter: **this body has carried a pail as a hundredweight for two months as a practice and not as a fact, and a clerk in another building has carried it as a hundredweight as a fact, and the two now agree, and agreeing is not the same as either of them being right** — and the count of one thousand and forty-five counted at a gate by four households over the first eleven days and one thousand and forty-five hundredweight on that same sheet for those same eleven days is **a coincidence and not a verification**. And the reader's sentence: **a body that cannot do the sum is a body that has a complaint; a body that can do the sum and cannot write the name is a body that has a figure, and a figure is a thing an office can use against a body in a room.** **The count of questions asked in a yard and not got an answer goes to three.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **161 — *She Came On The Fourth*** — days 274–275, the fourth and the fifth, a Sunday and a Monday. **A retired root engineer of fifty-six comes up the fen road in the rain on foot and is not announced, and the reason she was not announced is that she is already in this book's book as the first of the three names on the certificate in that room, and a body that announces at its own gate a person already on a page in its own book has admitted it does not know its own book.** She came by the ordinary post and walked the last nine miles, and the fen entered that as a fact and did not ask her about it. **She gives her name and her position in the first minute in a form that could be read back, and she says the fee before anybody offers it: nothing, and I am not charging you, and I am saying that first and not later, and a fee is the only thing a person in my position can charge and I have not charged it.** And the reason, which is the professional reason for the thing the reader of this body said in a yard eight days earlier: **a body that has been told its record cannot be used is a body that will start keeping another kind, and the other kind does not have a reading day and does not have an hour on it and is kept in a man's own book, and I have watched two bodies do that in nineteen years and one of them was a good body and the other one is the reason I am standing in yours.** Nobody thanked her and she said before she was thanked that she was not going to be; the count of that standing in a season is twelve. **The fen entered that it has not paid her, cannot pay her, and would not have been able to, and that this is the reason she came, in her own words and not improved.** The reader asks the one question nobody else in that yard can ask, giving the reason first: **are you here because of a declaration or because of a name.** Neither, and the third thing, and then she says she is not going to be forgiven and has not come to be thanked and has not come to be given a room, a bed or a figure. And then at the ninth hour the steward refuses her the seed house **in one sentence**: *a person who is not of this body does not sleep in the seed house* — with the reason entered, and **the reason is not suspicion, and is that an exception made this week is an exception made, and the next one is easier, and a seed house is not a place to put a custom in, and the same sentence would have been given to a licensed man off an office who had come up the fen road in the rain with a form in his bag.** She accepted it in about four seconds, which the fen counted, and **said nothing at all about it for the rest of the evening and was not thanked and did not ask to be.** On the Monday she stands at the wall and asks for the page, and the steward gives it to her without asking the reader or the clerk, and the reader enters that afterwards and has not written and asked why. And the reason she came, in her own words: **four sources, four hands, and not one of them is a clerk, and I have watched this holding be proud of that for eleven years and it is the single most useful thing I have ever seen a body do.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **162 — *The Name In Her Own Mouth*** — day 276, the sixth, a Tuesday. **A room with the bay doors shut and about eleven people in it, and a woman of fifty-six at the side of the table where the light is worst, and the man of about seventy is not in the room and the fen entered that it did not fetch him for the thirteenth time in a season because it has brought him out once in nine days and once in two days and is not going to do it a third time to find out what he would say about a word he has never heard.** She gives the four decisions in order and the number and then one word: **nineteen years ago she designed a safety relay for a flow in a dry country; the relay could have isolated a pulse going out where it should not have gone; she took the red line out of it; she changed the log entry from what it was to a line that said routine recalibration; she signed a report that put the cause down to salt creep and weather. Four thousand two hundred people in the first winter and nine thousand more moved. And then she said the name of the place, once, out of her own mouth, and did not say it again, and the clerk wrote it once and did not write it twice.** Then the reader asks what she wants this body to do with a number like that, and she says **nothing**, and wants that written down first, because everything else in that room has been about what people are going to do. And then the discipline: **we cannot check one word of it; there are two things in the world that can carry what she has said, one of them is her memory and the other is a record of compensation that is sealed and is produced to the person named in it on that person's own request, and no request has been made, nobody has been named, nothing has been opened, and it is not going to be opened in this room.** Tova Reed's standing, once, unnumbered: **a mechanism is not a verification and a soundness is not a hand, and this holding is about to enter the soundness of a woman into its own book and call the book a record.** And the cost. **She asks for the one thing she came for and it is not money: to be entered in this holding's own book, under her own name, with the date, as the person who said it — and the reason she gives is that in four years there is going to be one person who can say she said it, and if she is not on the page then the page says a thing happened to a room.** And the reader puts both halves in front of about eleven people and names the wrong half as wrong before he says it: **if this holding writes it down, an office can list it, and a thing in a list is a thing that has been had; and if it does not, then a woman said a thing in a room and it is gone, and in four years she will be the only person who ever said it and this book will be the proof that nobody was listening, and that is worse than the list.** **Enter it.** And the whole of the cost, in his own words, with his hand on the bench: **this body has been a name for a month and has just made itself a party, and I said the sentence about how that happens eight days before a woman walked nine miles to hand it to us, and I did not think about it for a day then and I have thought about it for two days since and I am not going to improve on it in a room with eleven people in it.** Nobody thanked anybody. Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **163 — *A Party That Named Itself*** — days 277–278, the seventh and the eighth, a Wednesday and a Thursday. **A return comes on the ordinary post, four lines, correct, and the third line has four words in it that are the name of a party, and a document is the only place a body can be a party.** Water supplied into the low quarter at no price between the second and the seventh, out of a source the return does not name, no price charged, the party named, the ordinary-course line: **a party supplying at no price is a party and is entered as one, and a party is not a holder, and a party has the standing of a party and not of a holder and not of an office. The name is the Pale Orchard.** Nobody in that room said the word *gift* and the fen entered that nobody said it and entered the word twice in its own book for the sole purpose of not using it. And the arithmetic, which is the second sum and the chapter's real argument: **the low quarter had five wells off on the fourth day of this month, and from the second to the seventh it has had the licensed supply at a shilling a pail and for every one of those six days water at no price out of a source nobody has named, and the number of pails in the second supply is in no book because there was no gate — I can add the two and I cannot divide them, and a figure that is the sum of two things one of which was never measured is not a figure, it is a shape, and I am not going to enter it and I am not going to be asked to.** And the three not-askings put side by side on one page on purpose: **this body's, over the penny; the trust's, over a figure carried by one person; the haulier's, over a holder's man with a book** — and a person in four years is going to read the three together and tell what sort of body this is. And then six sentences from a household's own mouth, from the low quarter: **the same four men were standing in that yard on the seventh and the sentence was gone, and one of the four said why, and the four words are: they gave us water, a person does not say a thing like that with water in the house; nobody at that gate asked her whether she still thought it, and he did not ask her, and the fen is glad, and a body being glad is not a column and there is no form for it.** And the man of about seventy fetched for the thirteenth time in a season, given the four lines and the two halves of the sum, and asked the only question in the room — **is water at no price better than water at a price** — which nobody can answer; he then said four words, **ask the giver's name**, and the fen does not know what they were about and has entered that it does not know. And the reader's position: **a body that cannot name a party on a form is now in a worse position than it was a week ago, because there is a party on a form that this holding cannot name either, and the two are going to be read in the same room one day by somebody who has not been born yet — and I am not going to say the second half and I have decided not to say it and that is a decision and not an oversight.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **164 — *A Holder In A Yard*** — day 279, the ninth, a Friday. **Garrow Nye, holder of record of the Pans well, of no address this office holds, comes up the fen road in the rain with a schedule in a leather bag and a man with him, and is let in at the gate and announced, because he has not been in this yard in his life and this holding has no custom for a charter holder and had to invent one at the gate in about four seconds.** About twenty-five people in his yard inside ten minutes. **He is not a liar and he corrects this holding twice in his first ten minutes, both against himself, and the reader enters the count and enters that the two are not to be improved on by anybody who was not in that yard:** the licensed draw on that well in the last twelve months is **one hundred and ninety thousand hundredweight** against a charter specification of **one hundred and seventy-four thousand**, and he has put the two in a room together and looked at them, and it is the first time in nineteen years; and **the man with the cart is licensed to carry under his charter, which he did not know until the morning he came up the road, and which is in the schedule in his bag and which he is not going to give out, because a schedule is a holder's document.** Then what he came to say, in five sentences: the well stopped at the fourth hour of the morning of the twentieth of last month and the book is at home and is anybody's book to read; **the flow under the low quarter and the flow under the Pans well are the same flow, and I do not know how a body of sixteen households finds that out and I have not asked how**; the man with the cart is not the cause of anything, I am; **and a form would have said it wrong and a form would have said it late, and I have had four days to write it down and have not written it down, and if you want to make a thing of it you are going to have to make a thing of it the hard way.** And then the reader puts the volume's frame back into a yard of twenty-five before the ask can take it out: **a charter holder is a supply and is not a thief, and nobody in that yard said the word *thief* about anybody during the ten minutes that man was speaking, and the fen did not find that out by asking.** Then the ask: **I want this holding to certify, on a form, that a flow is broken**, and the form is the ordinary form, correct, four lines, filled in with a date, a well, a licensed man and a number; **and he knows the form would close the licensed draw, which is the only supply that quarter has got, and that the water a party put in there at no price has stopped and nobody knows where it came from or where it went, and he has brought it in the rain anyway — a holder whose well is broken and who does not say so is a holder whose break is somebody else's water, and I have read four holders' books and can tell which of them were lying and I do not think I am one of them, and I would like that thought about with a form on it in front of twenty-five people.** And the batch's one Fieldbook panel, spent here, at the fourth hour, at the shaft in this holding's own low ground: **the use log's fifteenth line written first and read back first by the person who keeps the seed house**, a plain wire gauge test written down before the instrument was laid on the boards, four lines and not three — *The mouth is not the same twice. / A flow that is broken shows the break and not the hand that made it. / A person who says it out loud is not a finding. / Ask what it is carrying and not who is holding it* — **and the licensed man says out loud before he reads them that the second line is about a hand and not about a person and that no document in this book is going to quote them as an instruction or as a reason**, and the cost: the mark hot, the hand from the wrist down no use for about a day, the case carried up the slope by the man from the north row. And what he says up in the yard with twenty-five people in it: **this contact says nothing whatsoever about the Pans well, not one word of it, and the only man in this district who could tell me what is carrying under that floor is a man of about thirty-five who has said he will not be asked again by this body.** And the decision, at the seventh hour, entered and read back twice: **this holding will not put its name to the form and will not refuse to either; the form is on the bench; it has not been returned and it has not been torn up; the entry is that the form is on the bench and the answer has not been given; and the day the answer is given, a holder of record will have an answer from a body of sixteen households with no charter.** Panel: the one available, spent here. Notes: none.
- **165 — *The Eleventh*** — days 280–281, the tenth and the eleventh, a Saturday and a Sunday. **The tenth is a Saturday and nothing is read out in it. The eleventh is a Sunday and on the Sunday nothing happened that this body can see, and the fen entered that on the eleventh that it cannot say what happened and did not say the prediction was wrong and entered that it did not say it.** The standing figures of the day are read in the ordinary way with about nine people, none of them softened, **and the date is not on the list, and the clerk read a line under the list out of a standing instruction, and nobody in that yard asked what the line meant because about nine people in a fen of sixteen households knew what it meant.** The reader's reason, to nine people, with the second half before anybody can get to the first: **a prediction that comes and goes with nothing attached to it is not proved wrong by having nothing happen on the day; it is only proved wrong on a day when something does happen and it was not written down. A concealment was worth something on the twenty-fourth of last month, when the man doing it could not defend it and said so out loud to about four people in a room, and it is worth nothing today, and the man who did it is the one who has to say that, and he is in this yard, and I would like the clerk to enter that I said that in front of him and not behind his back.** Then the engineer of record, four sentences: **I said it to one person in a room and I would not write it, and the reason I gave at the time is that I could not defend it and I had not got a second reading, and that reason was a good reason on the twenty-fourth of last month and it is not a good reason today; I am not going to be thanked and I am not going to be forgiven today either, because it is not that kind of day; and I would like the clerk to enter a word nowhere in this book, in this entry or in any other, because nobody in this room is going to promise me anything.** The reader goes in and does not come out, and the seedwright of the trust says the chapter's sentence to nine people in the yard without him: **a thing that is true and in one room is not a secret yet, the day it is in the same room again is the day it is a secret — and here is the half I have not said in that room, and a thing that has been in one room for a month and has come true and has not been written down is not a secret, it is a debt; and I am not going to be the person you tell the next one to, and I am not going to be angry about it in front of nine people, and if anybody in this room wants to be angry about it in front of nine people I will help them and it will take about four minutes.** **She is not thanked and she did not ask to be, and the count of a sentence of that shape in a year is six, and the reader of this body was not in the room when she said it.** Then at about the fourth hour of the afternoon the man of about thirty-five comes down into the low ground on foot with nothing that was asked for: **I have been on that ground for nine days and there is more of it than there was on the twenty-second, and I am telling you that because you gave me a pail and I have not been paid and I said I would not be asked again — nobody asked me, I came down because I have got one count and I do not want it to be a thing I was asked for.** Nobody thanked him, **and the fen entered that the pail has not come back and the four hours have not been paid for and that the two of those are on the same page, and that the payment has arrived as information and this holding does not know what to do with a payment that arrives as information and is not going to put it in a column.** And one sentence that is not the word he has refused and is not an answer to anything — **it is not late** — and nobody in that low ground knew what that meant and the fen entered that it does not know and has not written and asked. Panel: none. Notes: none.

I am not the person you bring a thing to when it is not one, and you have known the difference between those two since the fourteenth of last month and so have I, and if you cannot hold the difference then you do not need me, you need a book, and you have one, and it is on the middle of this table and anybody may read it.** **The reader of this body was not in that room. The engineer of record did not answer her. Nobody in that room answered her. The time between the question and the end of the room is about nine seconds and the fen entered it and does not know what to do with it.** And then, at the seventh hour, in a yard of about nine, the other half, said out loud because a thing has to go into a yard before it is a thing everybody knows: **this holding has spent a month learning that a body with no standing can still be asked to put its name to a form, and a month learning that a man with a private record is a party, and it has not yet learned the third thing, which is that a person who is offered the job of being the one you tell is going to be offered it again, and is going to say no again, and the second no is easier and the third one is not.** Panel: none. The payment is this holding's own exposure and it is not hers and it went in this holding's book and not in hers.** And: **she is on this page once, she did not ask to be on it, she was not asked whether she wanted it and would have accepted it either way, and the clerk entered that and read it back and did not improve on it.** Then **the one observation the batch has available and the fifth in the chain: *the book cannot check her*** — entered on the clerk's own motion, unasked, and never explained. a form on a bench unanswered; the pail gone and the measure back; and the well on the shelf at five feet and one inch with no entry anywhere for it coming back, and a row, a wall and a yard four hundred miles off with no entry anywhere for any of the three.** And the rule read out in full again in a yard of about nine, **entered as read out three times in twenty-four days and used once, and the count of the uses is one.** And the reader's standing question, asked in the yard, and the fen's answer in six words: **I want somebody to say no** — **and the clerk did not read it back a second time, and the fen entered why, and the reason is that a thing read back twice is a thing that is going to be improved on, and that six words is not a standing and cannot be made into one, and that this holding has six things it has been told no by this season and has not been told no by anybody since the eighteenth of last month and has entered that it does not know which of those two facts it would rather be in.** Then the handoff at the north gate, in four sentences: **the fourth hour on the sixteenth of this month, four hundred miles off, a nail and a string and a woman of fifty-four's own hand; this holding has no standing on it, did not write and ask and is not going to; the reading is not in this book and is not going to be predicted in this book; and the fen entered the day and not the figure, and the day is the sixteenth, and the count of days between the end of this book and the fourth hour of that morning is one, and the fen entered that instead, because a day that can be counted is the only one of the three things this body is able to put in a book.** The **forty-fifth** section-nine note, dated the fifteenth, carrying the standing sentence.
