- **182 — *In Front Of People*** — day 308, the eighth, a Saturday. **At about the eleventh hour, in a full yard of about twenty-five people, the reader of this body said the thing he has been carrying since a room with the doors shut, standing up, and nobody made him.** He had told one person on the Thursday night that he was going to say a thing in that yard on the Saturday at the eleventh hour and had not said what it was, **and she asked him nothing about it, and the fen entered that a man who says out loud on a Thursday night that he is going to say something on a Saturday has given the yard the day and the hour and kept the thing.** The ordinary business of that hour carried on around it — two of them arguing about a gate post and the man of about fifty being told his cart shed roof was not going to last the month — and **the fen entered that none of it stopped, and that this is the first time in this book's history that something has been said out loud in a yard of about twenty-five people and the ordinary business of a Saturday carried on around it at the same time, and that he asked for the eleventh hour and not the fourth hour because at the fourth hour the yard is empty and at the eleventh hour it is full, and a thing said to nine people is a thing said to a room and a thing said to twenty-five is a thing said to a yard.** **He gives the date of the room, then the hour, then the number of people in it, in that order: the twenty-fourth of a month two months back, about the fourth hour of the afternoon, a room with the doors shut, four of them in it and one of them the clerk, who confirmed the hour out loud in the ordinary voice from his own hand before the reader of this body got to the fourth sentence.** **The thing, in about six sentences: he said it to one person and would not write it down; the reason he gave at the time is that he could not defend it and had not got a second reading, and that reason was a good reason then and is not a good reason today; the date it named fell on a Sunday, the eleventh of last month, on which nothing happened and there was nothing to be honest about; the man who did it is the one who has to say that, and he said it in front of him and not behind his back; and he is saying it in front of nine hundred people this morning, and there is nothing on this page to be honest about, and he would like that entered. THE FEN ENTERED THAT THE NUMBER IS NOT A COUNT AND DID NOT CORRECT IT, and gave the reason: a man making an apology is entitled to one wrong number about how many people are hearing him, and it is the only number in this book this holding is not going to check.** Then four more: **he did it to one person and not to a body; a thing that is in one room and not in a book is a thing that only one person can be asked to carry, and I made a person into a book, and I would not have done that to a stranger; and he wants it entered that he would not have done it to a stranger, and that the fact that he would not have done it to a stranger is not a defence and is the reason it was worse; and he asked for no forgiveness and said he would not be thanked and said it is not that kind of day.** **The clerk entered it and read it back in the ordinary voice and did not improve it. NOBODY THANKED HIM, nobody said a word, and the fen entered that nobody treated it as a thing between two people, and entered the reason: about twenty-five people watched a man say a thing out loud in daylight, and a thing said out loud in a yard is a fact about a yard and not a thing two people have.** She answered in one sentence, in the ordinary voice, at the wall side, to about twenty-five people and not to him, **and it was not forgiveness and it was not a refusal: I am not going to say that makes it right and I am not going to say it does not, and I am going to go on the road on Monday, and the reason I am going is on a page with my name at the top of it and not on this one, and I would like it entered that I said the reason is on another page.** She then sat on the bench in the cart shed and worked on the trust's list until the yard emptied, and nobody sat down with her. **She was not thanked, not forgiven on the page, and forgave nothing on the page, and the fen entered that nobody treated the answer as forgiveness and entered that nobody treated it as a refusal either and is not going to improve on the answer or find out which of the two it was.** Then, before the figures, **the reader of this body said he was not going to say that again this month, and gave the reason: a thing said once in a yard is a thing a man did and a thing said twice is a standing this holding would have to keep, and he has watched this holding get a standing it did not ask for out of a thing a man said once in a room.** And at the fourth hour the question went into a yard of about nine and nobody took it, and the fen entered that **the count of the times this body has asked it is three and answered never, and the count of the times it has been available to a room in this holding and not taken is six, three of which are this question, and both counts stand and neither has been added to the other.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **183 — *The Name Becomes A Person*** — days 309–310, the ninth and the tenth, a Sunday and a Monday. **On the ninth a letter comes up the fen road on the ordinary post, four lines, correct, on the party's own paper and not an office's**: the supply at no price made into the low quarter between the second and the seventh of last month **has not been resumed and the reason is not given and no reason is asked for**; **the party will be in the district on the tenth and a person will come to this holding on foot and will stand in whatever yard this holding keeps its book in**; that person is the person who signs these returns and his name is at the foot of the sheet, **and a party is a party and is not an office and has no standing over anybody**; and the fourth line, that it asks for no form, no certificate, no answer and no water. **It is a letter and it is not a return, and the fen entered the difference: a return is a thing an office keeps and a letter is a thing a person sends, and this holding has had four returns in two months and has never had a letter.** **On the tenth he comes up the fen road on foot at about the second hour of the afternoon, unannounced, and is announced before he speaks**, standing up in a yard of about eleven by the person who keeps the seed house, who says he is not of this body, is not on anything and is not a representative of anything, and that she is not going to start doing it differently for him. **He gives his name and his position in six sentences in a form that could be read back: MY NAME IS TARIN CALLOW. I AM THE PERSON WHO SIGNS THE RETURNS OF THE PALE ORCHARD. I HELD A POST IN THE DISTRICT WATER OFFICE AT FENNHERE FOR SIX YEARS AND I DO NOT HOLD ONE NOW AND I HAVE NOT HELD ONE FOR ELEVEN. I HAVE NO LICENCE AND NO CHARTER AND NO PAPER EXCEPT THAT ONE. I AM NOT A REPRESENTATIVE OF ANYTHING AND I AM NOT ANYBODY'S GUIDE.** **He is correct in every particular and the fen entered that on the day, and entered that a man being correct in every particular in a yard of about eleven people is a harder thing to write down than a man being wrong, and that this holding has far more practice at the second.** **And in the first ten minutes he corrects this holding, against the party and not against this holding, and says he does it in the first ten minutes so that nobody can think for the rest of the afternoon that he came to be liked: WE WERE NOT GIVING IT. THE SUPPLY WAS ALREADY PAID FOR. There is a line in our own accounts that says what it cost and I have not got it with me and I am not going to read you a figure I cannot show you. That is the correction. It is not a smaller thing than the one you have written down. It is a different thing, and it is worse, because what you have written down is that we did something for them and what is true is that we moved our own water through their quarter.** The fen entered that this is the first time in this book's history that a person has corrected this holding against his own interest, and that it does not settle anything. **Then the true thing, and it is true, and this holding has spent a year arguing against guessing and cannot answer one word of it: a controlled system does not fail the way an uncontrolled one fails; an uncontrolled system leaves people to find out, and the four wells in that lane went off on four different days in a month and every household worked out for itself what to do about it, some of them finding out before anybody else and some of them last, and a quarter of four hundred and forty-one people spent a month doing arithmetic about water with no instrument; and a system with a schedule and a rate and a class of use and a form does not do that, and a quarter that has a form on it is a quarter in which nobody has to guess where the water went, and you can go and read it, so can he, so can the man with the cart, and a page that is dated is worth more to a person with a fever than a well-informed neighbour.** **Then the method, not softened, at the same voice and the same speed, and he says he is not going to put it after the true thing to get the true thing said first: the schedule is made, the class is chosen, the people in the class are counted; a count is made of who is in a quarter so that the quarter can be supplied; and a quarter supplied on a schedule for a season has a supply that belongs to the supply and not to the people in it, and when the schedule changes the people in it are not a people any more, they are a class that has moved or a class that has not; and he knows what that sentence sounds like on the other side of a form, and has written it in a letter this week and had it not typed, and wants that on the page in his words and not in a summary.** Two of the eleven went out of the yard and nobody followed them, **and the fen entered why: a man who has just said a true thing and then said the thing the true thing is built on does not get followed out of a yard by a body that has learned something this month about letting people be finished.** **The demand, which is correct and is a document: that this holding will state, in its own book and on a date, the number of people in the low quarter, where they are, and how many of them there are. The reader of this body cannot refuse it and cannot accept it and said so out loud in one sentence, and the fen entered both separately: it cannot refuse, because a body that refuses a question in the open has said the question; it cannot accept, because this holding does not know the answer and has said so for two months in a room and in a yard and on a bench where a form is sitting unanswered; and the difference between those two is the whole argument of this volume in one line.** Then one question asked in the open with the reason first — **what the party is for** — and the checkable half in about four sentences: **a party is a set of people who have agreed to be answerable for one another's water; there were four of them at the start on a road out of a district where nobody was going to answer for anything, and they wrote it down and gave each other the right to be asked by a household that had nothing, and that was the whole of the invention and it is not clever and should not have taken a party to think of.** And the half he will not give: **why they are organized that way and what they intend to be in five years, and the reason is that it is not checkable, and that anything else would be four months of words that sound like a body admitting what it does not know and are not. The fen entered that the count of that refusal is one and entered that the count of one is a count of this morning and not a count of a man, and that it is not going to be carried forward as a standing.** He was not thanked, nobody was forgiven anything, and the reader of this body did not shake a hand and did not offer a chair. Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **184 — *What It Did, And What It Said*** — days 311–312, the eleventh and the twelfth, a Tuesday and a Wednesday. **On the eleventh a return comes up the fen road on the ordinary post, four lines, correct, the party's own return, reporting a death in its own operation in its own words in the ordinary course**: on the eighth, moving water into a quarter in which wells are off, **one man died, he was thirty-one, he is named in the return of the district and not in this one**; the manner was a fall of about nine feet onto stone while a pipe was being laid, and the party paid for the stone to be taken up and the ground made good **and did not pay for the man and could not**; the party reports the death against itself and does not report a cause and says in that line that it is not able to give a cause anybody could check; and the fourth line, that a party that reports a death in its own operation is a party and is entered as one. **Nobody lies in it and nothing is softened.** **The arithmetic, done in a yard because nobody would go back into the room: what this holding can check is three figures and a day, and she says she is not going to count them out loud because it would take forty minutes and make a spectacle of a dead man; what this holding cannot check is whether the schedule put him there, whether the count put him there, whether the rate and the class and the return made a man of thirty-one be on that road on that day with a pipe in his hands instead of somewhere else with a wage; the two are on one line and are not added together; and she says the sentence again anyway — a figure which is the sum of two things one of which was never measured is not a figure, and it is not going into this book, and this is the sixth time in two months that this holding has been beaten home by somebody else's arithmetic, and the count of six is entered and is not going to stop being entered.** **The death is on a page. There is no body in a room in this chapter and there was not one in a yard either, and the fen entered that the reader of this body did not ask a single question about the man and entered why: a man is thirty-one and dead on a piece of paper and the only thing this holding could offer him is a question.** **And in the evening, with the bay doors shut and about eleven people in the room, a woman of a household in the low acre came up the fen road in wet boots and sat down and did not take them off and nobody asked her to, and the trust's ledger was shut on the table in front of the seedwright of the trust and was not opened while that woman was talking, and the fen entered that it was shut by the person whose it is.** **Six sentences, entered entire, and she says both halves of what she came to say in the same breath and is not asked to choose: she is not going to talk about the man, she did not know him, and anybody who thinks she came up nine miles to be sorry has misunderstood the whole of the evening; she is here because the party is not wrong about the schedule and is wrong about the count, and she has worked that out on her own feet; A COUNT OF WHO IS IN A QUARTER IS A COUNT OF WHO CAN BE REACHED — you do not count a quarter so that you know the quarter, you count it so that you can get to it; my household was not in it and my household's man is one of the people it did not reach, and he is in the low acre and not in the low quarter, and he has been on the same road as those men every day of his life and is not on any page, and nobody counted him because there was no reason to count him; so both halves of that are true and she is not going to be asked to pick one, and the party is not a bad office, it is four people who did exactly what she has just described, correctly, in the order they had to do it in, got it wrong, knew they were getting it wrong, and wrote it on a page; and she is not here to tell anybody what to do about it and wants that said in her house's name and not her own, and is not going to name a person in that yard in the low acre, because she said on the twenty-second of last month that she did not want a body that is not a quarter to come, and has not changed her mind, and there is a difference between telling a thing in a book and bringing a body, and she is the one who has to carry her own door.** **And then the sentence the volume needs, said once, out loud, in the open, by a person who is not the accused and not the accuser: ANNEKE ROOS said, standing up, in the ordinary voice, THE ACCUSATION AND THE METHOD ARE TWO THINGS, AND WE HAVE BEEN ARGUING WITH ONE OF THEM FOR A MONTH.** Then the reader of this body's second half, which is the half he is going to be blamed for: **a method that counts who can be reached is a method that will reach the people it did not count the next time, and he says it out loud in this room because everybody in this room has already said it out loud to themselves, and there is no point in the ninth hour of the evening finding out who has been thinking it; and a thing said to yourself is a thing this body has a habit of, and it is not a good habit, and he has been in four rooms in two months where everybody knew what was happening and nobody had it written down, and he was in one of the four, and that is how a page about a man who is thirty-one and dead gets written and nobody ever has to answer for it.** Then the woman of the low acre asked, in the open, what this holding is going to do about it, and he gave the only honest sentence available: **it has no standing, no charter, no form on which to put that number, and no second reading of anything, and the count of the things this body does not know is four and is not going to be five this month because a man said a hard thing in a room; so it is going to write it down with the hour on it and read it back out loud in front of the people it is about; and those two things are worth very little, and a page is not a supply and a reading-out is not an answer, and the woman who asked is owed more than a page and this body cannot give her more than a page.** Nobody thanked anybody. Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **185 — *What Comes After The Stop*** — day 313, the thirteenth, a Thursday. **The second and last use of the standing rule in this volume, and the only draw in the batch, and the two are the same event.** At about the fourth hour in the low ground four hundred yards below the north gate, at the boards over a shaft that came off on the twenty-first of a month three months back and was put back together on the twentieth of last month, a draw is begun with a licensed man holding the book and the hour on it, and the reader of this body at the top of the slope with about nine people, **and he did not go down and gave the reason out loud before anybody asked him: a body that stands over a crew is a body the crew talks to, and this holding has four people on a floor and no custom for it, and he had been told that on the nineteenth of last month and has not improved on it since.** The man of the north row with the cough went down the ladder with the shovel three times in forty minutes, was told out loud that he was not to be asked to do it again, said nothing about that and did it anyway, **and the fen entered that a man who is told he is not to be asked and does the thing is not a man who has agreed to it and is not a man who has refused it either, and that the fen does not have a word for that and is not going to find one this month.** The return was read at the fifth hour of the evening of the twelfth and **the first line was established before the draw was begun, which the fen entered is the first time in the four years of that rule that it has been written down first, and the first line is kept and is kept first.** Nobody obstructed anybody, nothing was delayed, no door was shut in a face, entered separately as the correct conduct of a Thursday morning. Forty minutes of ordinary work, the level taken before and after and two numbers written side by side and **no difference written.** **The rule is read out in full, four lines, in the yard at about the fourth hour before any of that, and it is read out for the third time this month, and the count of the readings and the count of the uses are two counts and are not the same count, and the fen entered that a rule read out on the morning it is used is not a rule that is being kept, and that the mornings it is not used are the ones this body would have to give up first.** The draw is begun at about the half hour past four and is entered as the second in this volume and the last. **At four feet the licensed man called the stop out loud, in the ordinary voice, from the head of the shaft, to about four people on the boards; two of the men stopped before he had finished the sentence, which the fen entered, because a stop is a stop and the half second in which it is not yet obeyed is not a failure of the rule and is not going to be written down as one; and the stop was entered by whoever held the book, which was that licensed man, in his own hand at the head of the shaft with the hour on it, and the clerk entered the same thing in this holding's book and read it back down the slope so that the four people on the boards heard it entered.** **The rule is satisfied. Every one of the four lines is satisfied. Nobody has broken anything and nobody has a defence, and the fen entered that this is the second use in this volume and the last and that the count of the uses is now two and is not going to be three. AND THE DRAW GOT NO LINE IN THE USE LOG AND THE CHAPTER SAYS SO ON THE PAGE: a line records a contact and never a reading, a draw gets no line, a hold gets no line, the log stands at fifteen lines, and the two contacts since the ninth of last month and the hold in between have got no line either, and the reason the log stands at fifteen is that this holding cannot write down what it did on the boards in a line anybody could check.** **Then the thing no rule in this book has ever been about, said out loud on the slope with about nine people standing in it: nine people came up that slope at about the fourth hour to see whether a thing could be got through to a road, and their names are in the book and he is not going to read them out and is not going to count them, because a count would be a thing they did not come for; THEY DID NOT GET IT — the draw stopped at four feet, the four lines were satisfied, the book says what happened, and about four hundred yards of a road on the other side of that ground did not open, and every part of it was correct; and then THE SENTENCE: WE HAVE WRITTEN A RULE ABOUT WAITING AND WE HAVE CALLED IT A RULE ABOUT CARE. ANY BODY CAN OBEY IT PERFECTLY FOR EVER AND NEVER DO A THING AGAIN AND IT WILL LOOK EXACTLY LIKE A BODY THAT IS BEING CAREFUL. And that it is the second time this book has said that sentence, the first having been in a room in this building with about eleven people in it, the day not given, the clerk entering that he did not say the day.** The nine are entered by what they came for and not by name: a woman of a household in the low acre whose household's man was told on the Sunday; a driver on the road the carts went onto, who came up with them on the Friday; a second driver's household; a woman of a household in the low quarter; and the man of about fifty's household, which is at the top of that slope most days of its life. **One of them has a fever, he is not one of the nine, he is a household in the low acre, and he is not the reason the nine came up; and one of the nine has lost a day of carrying that is not going to be repaid in anything, in money or in seed or in a week, and the reader of this body looked for about four minutes for a way to repay it and there is not one, and the fen entered that he looked.** **The arithmetic, said out loud on the slope, derived twice, the two agree, and the examiner took the second through a third with her finger on the page after saying out loud that she keeps time and does not round: one day of a licensed man this month, the thirteenth, at one pound a day, is twenty shillings, which is one pound; and four pounds and fivepence is eighty-five shillings, less twenty, is sixty-five shillings, which is three pounds and five shillings, and in pence a thousand and twenty less two hundred and forty is seven hundred and eighty pence, which is sixty-five shillings, which is three pounds and five shillings. And she says the next part faster this month and does not split it: A COST THIS HOLDING CAN COMPUTE IS A COST IT CAN HAND TO AN OFFICE — said in a room a month ago and on the first of this month and a third time now, and she is not going to be glad about it and is not going to be sorry about it, and nobody is going to thank her for it.** Then **the cost, in the engineer's own hand, in a line of its own, at the ninth hour in the cart shed with the door open and the clerk standing in it: THE MARK IS HOT. THE HAND FROM THE WRIST DOWN WAS NO USE FOR ABOUT A DAY. A HEADACHE BEHIND THE EYES FROM ABOUT THE SEVENTH HOUR LAST NIGHT UNTIL ABOUT THE FOURTH HOUR THIS MORNING, WHICH IS NOT THE MARK AND IS NOT A MARK AND IS NOT TO BE ENTERED AS ONE. FOUR FEET. And on the same line, in the clerk's hand: the four accounts of the arm stand where they stood, THIS IS NOT A FIFTH ACCOUNT AND IT DOES NOT RECONCILE ANY OF THEM.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **186 — *What The Road Is For*** — days 314–315, the fourteenth and the fifteenth, a Friday and a Saturday. **The man of the north row with the cough walks out to the low quarter at about the fifth hour on the Friday and back at about the seventh hour of the evening and comes into a yard of about nine without sitting down and has two things and asks nobody anything about either**, and the fen entered that he did not and that nobody tried to make him. **The first, in four sentences in the plainest words he has: THE PAILS HAVE GOT LONGER AND THE WALKS HAVE NOT — whatever is going on, the water is further off than it was and the distance a person walks to it is exactly what it was; the quarter is not being supplied on a charter, it is being supplied on a class, and a charter is a thing somebody can point at and a class is a thing somebody has been put in, and the four that stopped saying it and the one that started asking who is paying are all still in those houses and nobody out there has been told a word about any of this week; and there is a second man with a cart in that lane, he is not the man with the cart, he has been on that lane four days, he does not come from this district, and nobody knows where his water comes from and the man did not ask, and the fen entered that he did not ask and entered the reason, which is the same one as last time: it is not my row.** Nobody in that yard said anything about the second cart, and the fen entered that he said a man was on a lane and did not say a word about how he got the water, and that those two halves are in this book and are not to be joined up by anybody in four years. **The second, smaller, in four sentences: the household that has been counting its own pails at a gate for eleven years was told on the fourth of this month, by the officer with the book, in a yard of about twenty-five people, that a gate count is not a record; he was not being cruel, he was doing his business, it is not one of the four lines on his sheet and it is not wrong, and it is going to be in a room somewhere in about four years and this holding has entered it and does not know where; and that household kept the count anyway, every day, and on the morning of the fourteenth the woman of that household got up at the fourth hour and walked up this road with nine years of it in a sheet in her own hand, one line a month, and stood in this yard at about the seventh hour and gave it to the clerk and said she would like it entered, and it is entered, and she did not want anything else and she did not stay; and she counted pails for eleven years for her own house and counted them again on that morning for a body she is not part of and has never been asked to be, and nobody in that yard asked her to, and the count is on the page and it is in her hand and not in anybody else's.** A line of it: **a date at the left, a number at the right, nothing in between, the numbers all three figures or all two, and the hand does not change in nine years except once, in the fourth year, where a five has been made into a three and the three made over the five, and there is no note, and the woman said the fifth one is the one she is not sure of and she is leaving it as it is.** **The batch's second sum, said out loud with the bay doors shut on the Friday night, not asked for, with the word before the figure: I AM GOING TO DO A SUM I DID NOT WANT TO DO, AND I HAVE NEVER IN MY LIFE NOT WANTED A SUM, SO I AM GOING TO SAY THAT OUT LOUD FIRST, AND I AM GOING TO DO IT BECAUSE A SUM IS FOR DOING AND NOT FOR WANTING. Two hundred and fourteen pails for a month at sixteen pence the hundredweight, being three thousand four hundred and twenty-four pence, derived twice and agreeing — two hundred and fourteen at a shilling is two thousand five hundred and sixty-eight pence and two hundred and fourteen at fourpence is eight hundred and fifty-six, and the two come to three thousand four hundred and twenty-four; three thousand four hundred and twenty-four pence is two hundred and eighty-five shillings and four pence, which is fourteen pounds five shillings and fourpence. And the part she did not want, said in a room and not in a yard: that figure is the only number on that sheet, that sheet is eleven years of a household counting its own water at its own gate in its own hand, and this holding has taken four words off the top of it and turned it into a rate this holding can hand to an office; that household asked for the count to be entered and did not ask for it to be priced; I have priced it; nobody in that room stopped me; the woman who keeps the money did not say one word about it while I did it and said one word about it afterward. ANNEKE ROOS, WHO IS THE WOMAN WHO DOES THE SUMS, SAID THE WORD. SHE SAID NOW. She said it once and did not elaborate and was not thanked and did not ask to be, and the fen entered that the woman who priced it said the word and that nobody in that room could have stopped her and that she did not need stopping and that the two of those facts are on the same line.** **Then the sentence that is the chapter: A FIGURE THAT A BODY CANNOT CHECK IS NOT A PROTECTION. IT IS A DEBT. And this holding has had those four for a month and this month we found out whether a form helps, and a form does not help. They are the same four, named: what that quarter drinks now; the strip about two paces wide in front of four houses and what comes up out of it; the eleven a man gave in a yard on the twenty-seventh of last month, which is a number of the ones who came to a decision and not a number of anybody; and what a man spent on his own ground eleven miles off and has not written down and is not going to. And they are not one more than they were on the first of this month and not one fewer, and the count of four figures this holding cannot check and the count of the four things this body does not know are two different counts and are still not to be run together, and she has said that twice this season and is saying it a third time.** **Then the fault line, out loud, at about the eleventh hour on the Saturday in a yard of about nine, with the standing rule read out in full before the figures were closed and the count of the readings in this month entered at four and the count of the uses at two and the two counts declared to be two counts: THE FAULT LINE IN THIS BODY USED TO BE BETWEEN TWO PEOPLE. THEN IT WAS BETWEEN A BODY AND A JOB. AND IT IS NOW BETWEEN A BODY AND A CLASS, and the reason the third is worse is that two people can refuse each other, a body can refuse a job and we have watched that happen and it cost us a woman and a book and it was survivable, AND A CLASS CANNOT BE REFUSED — a class is a thing an office puts on a form, and this body cannot get out of one by refusing it, because refusing a form is not a thing anybody can do twice. And he put this holding in that class in his own hand on the fourth of this month and would do it again, and the reason he would is that the alternative was being put in it by somebody else, and he has never worked out which of the two he would rather have and has had a month to try.** Panel: none. Notes: none.
- **187 — *The Twentieth*** — days 316–320, the sixteenth through the twentieth, a Sunday through a Thursday. **The twentieth, a Thursday, is the last working day this batch owns, and at about the eleventh hour the standing figures are read out whole in a yard of about nine with nothing softened.** The compost line for the tenth month at eighty pounds on four hundred hundredweight at four shillings, derived twice and agreeing, the ninth month's figure also eighty pounds and the two on the same line, **the run at ten not discharged in ten, a figure that repeats entered as a worse kind of figure than a figure that moves, the word crowded, and the word and the figure not agreeing.** **The compost line for the eleventh month NOT ENTERED with the reason entered, the figure falling on the first of next month, which is a Saturday, and the eleventh month of a run of eleven not discharged in eleven once that figure is in.** The leak at three-quarters of an inch, read on the twenty-first of a month two months back, no verdict on the difference from the thirteenth of a month three months back, not measured since, not to be measured again. **The beat not logged since, cause not established, column open, the column not opened in front of nine people and the not opening entered as a decision and not an oversight, and the fen entered that the day of that beat is not restated in this book and is not going to be.** **The seventh column at thirty-five, the last reading day of this month the thirtieth, which is not this batch's, and the count has stood at thirty-five since the first because the door is read on the first and the thirtieth of a month and has been for four years.** **The boards at two hundred and fifty-four days, day minus sixty-six, and the March's tin at three hundred and one days, day minus nineteen, both read out loud by the clerk before either number, which he has now done on nine reading days running and which nobody has asked for on any of the nine.** **The standing rule four lines, satisfied on the third of a month five months back, used twice in this volume, on the twenty-second of a month two months back and on the thirteenth of this month, count of the uses two and not going to be three.** The use log at fifteen lines, the fifteenth a contact on a boarded floor on the ninth of last month, **and entered on the same standing entry and not in the log, because none of them is a line: a second contact on the twentieth of last month, a hold on the same boards on the twenty-fourth of last month, and a draw on the thirteenth of this month.** **The rootmark four inches, branching twice, unchanged, no second mark, the burn not a mark, and four accounts of that arm none of which agrees with any of the others, and the draw of the thirteenth is not a fifth account and reconciles none of them.** The form on a bench, correct, filled in, not returned, not torn up, answer not given. **The well on the shelf at five feet on the sixteenth of last month, four feet against the sixteenth of a month six months back, not decomposed, and no entry anywhere for that well coming back, with the day letter, the man with a spade, and the fourth line with the two numbers this body did not add up.** **Then the standing rule read out again in full, four lines, in the same yard, before the figures were closed, because a rule read only when it is used is a habit and this one is not a habit — and the fen entered that it has now been read out in full five times in this month and used twice, and that the two counts are two counts and are not the same count, and entered that the rule says nothing whatever about what comes after the stop, and that on the thirteenth nine people came up a slope and a road did not open, and every one of those four lines was satisfied the whole time and not one of them was about the nine.** Then the change, read out because a month of standing is not closed by a column: **the seed side is on a road, the water is on a form, a man eleven miles off is a supply and not a thief and has been said in that yard four times and will not be said a fifth, a man of about thirty-five will not say a name and has refused four times in nineteen years, a thing under a low quarter will not be drawn from and eleven came up a road and said so in a yard and gave a figure that is not a number of anybody; a party has become a person, and the person said a true thing about a form and a quarter that this holding has spent a year arguing against and cannot answer one word of, and said the method out loud after the true thing and not before it, and he was not thanked and nobody was forgiven anything; and this holding has four figures it cannot check and a form it has not answered and a cart it will not ask about, and every one of those is entered and none of them is thanked, and he has come to the end of that list and is not going to add a fifth thing to it in a yard to see how it reads.** **Then the man of about seventy is fetched at about the fourth hour, the fifteenth time in a season, given the figures and the counts in that order, asked for the last one to be repeated, and says four words: ASK WHO COUNTS THEM.** Nobody answered him and nobody asked him what it was about, **and the fen entered that it does not know and is not going to write and ask, and entered that in fifteen times it has never twice been about the same thing.** Then the handoff at the north gate at about the seventh hour, in about nine people, four sentences: **the first of next month is a Saturday, and it is the day the compost line for the eleventh month falls on, and this holding does not know what that figure is, and the door has a column and a month and a figure, and this body has no standing on any of the three; it did not write and ask and is not going to, and the fen entered the day and not the figure, the way it entered the day and not the figure for a shelf four hundred miles off; and that is the third clock this body owns that it can count and cannot price, and he is not going to make a column out of the three of them, and is not going to say the word pattern out loud in this yard about any of them, and the clerk entered that he did not.** Nobody so much as one word was said. **And the forty-eighth note under section nine, dated the twentieth, signed by nobody but Marek, read back before it was initialled, there is no charter, and the note says so on its face, carrying the standing sentence: THIS IS WHAT A MONTH OF A VOLUME IS.** Panel: none. Notes: the **forty-eighth**, dated **the twentieth**, **carrying the standing sentence.**

## Volume 04 Batch 0005 — Chapters 188–196, Movement 5, *The Long Pan* (drafted)

- **188 — *The Wrong Day In The Book*** — days 321–323, the twenty-first, the twenty-second, the twenty-third, a Friday, a Saturday, a Sunday. **The reader of this body reads this holding's own book at about the third hour on the twenty-first and finds that he has been keeping a date four hundred miles off out of his own head for eleven years while a certified copy of the schedule of readings lay on the seed house table the whole time; and then, shortly before the fourth hour, in a yard of about eleven people, he reads out that the next ordinary reading is on the first of next month, which his own hand calls a Saturday. GAEL SENN, the examiner from the district, is a woman who keeps time, and she says out loud, before anything is written down, that the first of next month is a Monday and not a Saturday and that she keeps time and does not round, and the day number is the first of next month and is not in question. The day number is wrong too, because the well on that shelf is read on the sixteenth of every month and not on the first of any month.** Both figures are entered, neither is improved on, and the count of the two days this book has got wrong in its own hand is now two and is not reduced. The tenth reading was taken four hundred miles off on the sixteenth, at the fourth hour, by the occupier, with her own nail, in her own yard, on her own wall, and **this holding has no standing on that ground, did not write and ask, and is not going to, and the figure is not on this page and is not going to be.** The four lines of the standing rule went down that road at that household's own cost and arrived on or about the twentieth. **The count of three day-and-not-the-figure entries stands at three and does not come down, and the fen enters that one of the three was aimed at a day that was not a reading day at all and that this is not an improvement on the other two.**
- **189 — *A True And Narrow Thing*** — days 324–326, the twenty-fourth, the twenty-fifth, the twenty-sixth, a Monday, a Tuesday, a Wednesday. **The form on the bench in the seed house is answered in the SECOND box and not the first.** The first box asks whether a supply is broken; the second asks what a body did about it and in what quantity. **It is a true and narrow thing and the fen enters that the narrowness is the whole of what he has this month.** Returned with the counter's mark, the hour and the name of the clerk who copied it, and the original never returned and never torn up and on the bench since **the twenty-seventh of last month**, and the copy cost four pence a sheet at the engineer of record's own cost. **Consequence, entered the same day: an office in the ordinary course reduced the licensed draw at the Pans well by a fifth on the twenty-sixth, and the reduction is correct, and the holding did not appeal it and did not ask why.**
- **190 — *Three Places And Three Numbers*** — days 327–329, the twenty-seventh, the twenty-eighth, the twenty-ninth, a Thursday, a Friday, a Saturday. One pail, one stopwatch, one rod, one line, three places, three numbers: **one hundred and forty-six seconds, two hundred and two, one hundred and eighty-eight — the third faster than the second, and nobody improved on it.** The plan drawn on the twenty-ninth of a month two months back at the ninth hour of the evening, without standing on the ground, is wrong in its second half mile and is south of where it should be. **A rise of eleven feet in two hundred yards, which is about one in fifty-five, and the chapter says out loud that a grade of that slope is walkable for two hundred yards and not for a mile and a half.** A trial channel four feet long held an inch for an hour and a half. **The corridor's own volume is put down as a number and derived twice, the two agreeing: nine hundred yards by forty at two inches is two thousand cubic yards, which is three million three hundred and seventy-five thousand pounds, which is about thirty thousand hundredweight — and the comparison with the ninety-five a day is refused, and the refusal is the beat.** A gate is opened by a licensed man under a form and **is not a draw**, and the use log gets no line, and the fen says why out loud: a line records a contact and never a reading.
- **191 — *A Constant Times A Constant*** — days 330–332, the thirtieth, the first, the second, a Sunday, a Monday, a Tuesday. **The month turns overnight and the eleventh month's compost line falls on the first, at about the eleventh hour, in a yard of about twenty-five — which is the only day its own notice allows.** Four hundred hundredweight at four shillings is one thousand six hundred shillings, which is eighty pounds, derived twice out loud and the two agreeing, the second derivation at forty-eight pence a hundredweight being nineteen thousand two hundred pence, being two hundred and forty pence eighty times over. **It is the third consecutive month of eighty pounds and the run is eleven not discharged in eleven.** The word before the figure was *crowded*, and **a constant multiplied by a constant is not a measurement of anything outside that door**, and the figure and the word have never disagreed and are not going to be made to. The seventh column is read **thirty-six on the thirtieth and thirty-seven on the first, a day apart**, and the rule is not changed. The standing rule is read out in full in that same yard before the figures are closed — **six times across two months, five of them in the last month and this one in this one** — and its **count of uses is two and is not going to be three.** The month's costs go on four separate lines and are not folded into the shortfall. **The woman who does the sums says *crowded* again and this time says what it means: the figure has been the same for three months because the specification has not changed and the valuation has not changed, so the eighty pounds is a constant multiplied by a constant, and the word and the figure never disagreed because they were never about the same thing, and she is not glad about it, and a debt that nobody else owes is a debt this holding invented, and she says she was able this morning, and that it is thirty days from the first of last month, and that she is not going to stand in a yard and say that thirty days is quick.** The holding itself reads the third line as though it said *in a yard*, and the notice does not say it.
- **192 — *The Water Goes Where The Ground Says*** — days 333–335, the third, the fourth, the fifth, a Wednesday, a Thursday, a Friday. **The climax.** At about the fourth hour on the fourth, a licensed man opens the head of this holding's own ground under a form and a rate, writes the hour and the figure in his own book, and the fen stands at the top of the slope and does not go down. Four people carry water into the pan in pails and cut a channel and stand over the crew, which is a thing this holding has no custom for. **The corridor the sheet describes is three hundred yards south of where it was drawn, and the fen measured it himself on the plan and got the same three hundred yards, and the page has the hour on it and the hour is his own.** The rise is one in fifty-five and the ground goes the other way from the drawing. **A hold for four was put on it and the count of people who can hold a pattern for four is one and is public and does not change.** Coll Renner says the professional thing once, to the four men and to the engineer of record and to nobody else, before he packs the case.
- **193 — *Roald Trench And Sena Wick*** — days 336–339, the sixth, the seventh, the eighth, the ninth, a Saturday, a Sunday, a Monday, a Tuesday. **A stone-and-turf seed vault of forty households, four hundred yards off the north edge of the pan, built at their own cost in a month three months back, with no holder and no charter and no form on which anybody can be asked about it, on ground the district calls Crown-held and has never held, goes under at about the seventh hour of the ninth.** **ROALD TRENCH, of about forty-four years, and SENA WICK, of about thirty-eight years, are named out of a woman's hand and neither is of this holding and neither is a member of anything.** The vault is not recovered. **This holding was not there and did not ask and has not been asked, and a thing in a woman's hand about the north side is not in this book and this holding did not ask for it.** **The corridor is three hundred yards on the fourth, three hundred and eighty-four at about the eleventh hour on the eighth — sixteen short of the vault — and four hundred and eighty-six at about the seventh hour of the evening on the ninth, and the two speeds are derivable twice from those figures: eighty-four yards in the four days from Thursday to the Monday is twenty-one yards a day, and a hundred and two yards in the thirty-two hours from the Monday at the eleventh hour to the Tuesday at the seventh hour of the evening is seventy-six and a half yards a day, and the reason it went at twenty-one yards a day and then at seventy-six and a half is not established, and the fen says he does not know which of those two numbers is the water and which of them is the ground and is not going to guess at it in a yard.** A man of about thirty-five, **Soren Rill**, comes up the dry road on foot on the ninth, is announced in a yard before he speaks, gives his name and his position and the one thing only he can say about that ground, and does not stay, is not paid and is not thanked. **The man of the north row with the cough comes up the road at about the ninth hour of the evening of the ninth with about two hundred people behind him and says that a thing is in a woman's hand and not in this book, and is not asked for it, and does not give it up.**
- **194 — *Soldiers On The Dry Road*** — days 341–343, the eleventh, the twelfth, the thirteenth, a Thursday, a Friday, a Saturday. **Four soldiers and a man with a schedule walk the corridor that four hundred and eleven people crossed on the fourth.** The road is held from the fourth hour to the fourth hour of the day after tomorrow, the holding of it is in the schedule and is not discretionary, the class is **migration** and the rate is **fourpence the hundredweight**, and the office asks a party for the figure of the goods carried in the last six days and says the figure is not known. The arithmetic is done out loud in a yard: six hundred hundredweight at fourpence is two thousand four hundred pence, which is ten pounds; at sixteen pence it is forty pounds; **the difference is seven thousand two hundred pence, which is thirty pounds a week, and the thirty pounds is what the two prices are arguing about and not what anybody earns.** **The officer of the district says ten pounds and is right, and no office in this volume is anything but correct. The woman of the sums says twenty-four hundred pence is two pounds, stops in the rain, and says it out loud that she is wrong and that the officer said ten pounds before she did and did not look at her when she got it wrong, and an office does not put a party right on a question the party has not asked it. The count of wrong sums said in public is two and the first was eight days in a month at a gate.** The thirty pounds a week is a shilling on every hundredweight anybody moves over that corridor. **The office says it will ask a party for a figure it does not have, because that is what a form is for, and that a party which does not have the figure writes down that it does not have it, and that that is a complete answer and it is not a refusal and it is not a finding. The man of about fifty writes it, the officer reads it back, nobody is charged with anything, and the road opens by the seventh hour.**
- **195 — *Four Lines And A Refusal*** — days 344–346, the fourteenth, the fifteenth, the sixteenth, a Sunday, a Monday, a Tuesday. **A cross-region seed agreement on the trust's own paper, in the seedwright's own hand, in a yard of about twenty-five, read out and read back with the hour on it, four lines, and nothing in it is a finding against any person.** The third clause carries **a *seat* for a body of one and one body of two and a *seat* is not a licence to hold a pattern for four and is not a Stage and is not a body.** **The refusal clause names the cost out loud: Thornwild and the Assemblies, and both words are in the document and are the price of the seed, and the fen does not pretend the price was not named.** **Four hundred at a shilling and fourpence is sixteen pence, is six thousand four hundred pence, which is twenty-six pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence; four hundred at fourpence is six pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence; the difference is exactly twenty pounds, and the exactness is the whole of what is being said, and it is a carriage rate on a season and not a supply and not a wage and not anybody's living.** **A figure this holding computed has come out better than the same figure cost in the third of last month, for the first time, and the woman who does the sums says she does not know what to do with it and is not going to find out this month.** A low quarter states **four hundred and forty-one** in its own book, in its own hand, on its own page. **The eleventh reading of the well on the shelf is taken at the fourth hour on the sixteenth, a Tuesday, by the occupier, with her own nail, in her own yard, on her own wall, in wall order, and it is FIVE FEET. THE FOUR LINES GO DOWN THE FOUR-DAY ROAD AT THAT HOUSEHOLD'S OWN COST ON THAT DAY AND THIS HOLDING DOES NOT HAVE THEM YET, AND THE ENTRY IS OF WHAT HAS HAPPENED AND WHAT HAS NOT. IT DOES NOT HAVE THE TENTH, AND THE OCCUPIER REFUSES TO WRITE IT INTO A SHEET IN HER OWN HAND, BECAUSE A BODY FOUR HUNDRED MILES OFF THAT HAS SPENT A MONTH FINDING OUT IT WAS AIMING AT THE WRONG DAY IS NOT GOING TO BE HANDED A NUMBER BY A WOMAN IT HAS NEVER MET, AND THE WALL SHOWS THE GAP, AND THE WALL READS *AND THEN THE ONE I AM NOT WRITING, AND THEN THIS ONE*. The chapter ends on the sixteenth with the sheet on the road and the figure not in this building, and the reader says *four days*, and the road is four up and four down, which is eight. THE READING-OUT, THE CLERK'S ENTRY AND *Five feet and five feet* ARE NOT IN THIS CHAPTER: THE FIGURE ENTERS THIS HOLDING'S BOOK ON THE TWENTIETH OF THE TWELFTH MONTH, A SATURDAY, AT ABOUT THE NINTH HOUR OF THE MORNING, IN CH 196, WHERE IT BELONGS. There is a month between the two figures it has that is on no line in this book, and nobody in that yard wrote and asked for it, and there is still no entry anywhere for that well coming back.**
- **196 — *The Bottleneck, Said Twice*** — days 347–350, the seventeenth, the eighteenth, the nineteenth, the twentieth, a Wednesday, a Thursday, a Friday, a Saturday. **The seedwright's condition is paid, and it is paid exactly.** She set it in a yard on the twenty-sixth of a month two months back and refused to name the person; **the person was named on the fifteenth of this month by the woman of the low acre, and she named him to the man of about fifty and not to the fen.** He is the man of the north row with the cough, about sixty-eight. He was asked twice and said no once and yes once. **A hold for four was made and put in the book, so the count of people who can hold a pattern for four is TWO and the fen cannot do the second thing and does not know who can, and neither of them knows it is a count of people and not of skill.** The schedule and the rule are written out without Marek, because he was not in the room and nobody sent for him. **The question this book has carried goes into the book unanswered: that question is available and not taken twice and asked once, and the standing count of the questions available to a room in this holding and not taken goes from six to seven, and neither is added to the other, and the fen says there are three counts and that nobody in this book has ever added one of them to another.** **AT ABOUT THE NINTH HOUR OF THE MORNING OF THE TWENTIETH, A SATURDAY, THE FOUR LINES COME DOWN THE FOUR-DAY ROAD IN A LEATHER BAG BY THE ORDINARY POST, WRITTEN AT THE FOURTH HOUR OF THE MORNING OF THE SIXTEENTH AT THAT HOUSEHOLD'S OWN COST, AND THE READER OF THIS BODY READS THE WHOLE OF IT OUT IN A YARD OF ABOUT NINE, THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY IS APPOINTED READER, IT IS READ BACK, THE HOUR GOES ON IT, AND THE READER SAYS *Five feet and five feet* AND SAYS WHICH TWO: the ninth was five feet on the sixteenth of a month two months back and the eleventh is five feet on the sixteenth of this month, and there is a month between those two on no line in this book, and the two figures it does have are the same figure, and a figure which repeats is a worse kind of figure than a figure which moves.** The standing figures are read at about the eleventh hour of the twentieth in a yard of about nine with nothing softened. **The standing rule is read out in full for the sixth time and its count of uses is two.** A man of about seventy is fetched for the **sixteenth** time and **says nothing at all.** The bottleneck sentence is said **twice, on purpose, and the fen says out loud that he is saying it again and why.** The clerk makes the one observation this volume spends on a person: **the corridor this holding built is three hundred yards from the corridor this holding drew, the plan is on the page with the hour on it, the road it made is not a road, the vault that went under was four hundred yards from a door this holding did not open, and the reader of this body has not written down what any of that means, and this holding has been arguing since the first month of this book that a thing on a page is a thing somebody can check, and it has not checked this.** **The forty-ninth section-nine note is entered, and the number of entries that ask for nothing and wait for a year is forty-nine and that is a year and a day and it is not going to be rounded.**

# VOLUME 04 — THE CLOSE, CHAPTERS 148–196: WHAT THE CLOSE CHANGED ON THE PAGE

**The close audited all forty-nine chapters, recomputed every figure from the files, and repaired sixty-four lines in thirty-five of the forty-nine chapters. It wrote no new prose, added no sentence to reach a word count, replaced no scene and moved no beat. THE CHAPTER SUMMARIES ABOVE ARE THE CHAPTERS' SUMMARIES AND THEY STAND; WHAT FOLLOWS IS ONE LINE PER CHAPTER THE CLOSE TOUCHED, WITH THE LINE NUMBERS OF THE CHAPTER AS IT NOW STANDS, AND NOTHING FOR THE CHAPTERS IT DID NOT TOUCH. THE FINDINGS FILE IS `reviews/volume-04.findings.md` AND THE FULL REPAIR LIST, IN ITS OWN NUMBERING, IS IN `state/continuity.md` UNDER *VOLUME 04 — THE CLOSE*.**

**Batch 0001, six chapters touched.** **Ch 150:49** — `thirty` of our own households on this head is **sixteen**, which is the same sentence's own figure and the holding's count everywhere else. **Ch 152:7** — *the only thing in this chapter that makes the other two things mean anything* becomes **in this day's work**, the narrator's first sweep site. **Ch 153:47** — *the reason the whole of this volume is about* becomes **this season is about**, which is the diegetic frame and not a book-keeping one. **Ch 154:55** — `thirty` households on the head is **sixteen**; **:77** — the standing rule's satisfaction, two months back, is **three months back**; **:84** — *used once, on the twelfth of a month two months back* becomes ***the fourteenth of last month***, and this is the repair that **removed a third asserted use of a rule whose volume ledger says the count is two and is not going to be three**. **Ch 155:17** — *at about the fifth hour and forty minutes* becomes **the fourth hour and forty minutes**, against a draw begun at four twenty and the clerk's own entry at :23; eighty minutes was never on the page. **:87** — *I have read ground for nineteen years* becomes **nine years**, the outline's figure for reading ground and the only family in which nineteen was ever a slip. **Ch 156:19, :21, :91** — see the fix pass below for :19; :21 is the second of the two genuine *read ground* sites; **:91** was a bare `""` on a line of its own, the only such line in forty-nine files, and is deleted.
